claim: Hydractinia echinata is a common colony-forming cnidarian in the European North Atlantic.
source: In this study, we show that Hydractinia echinata, which is a common colony-forming cnidarian in the European North Atlantic (Figure 1), provides a powerful model system to study the cellular and molecular basis of animal regeneration.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the geographic distribution and colonial nature of the organism.

claim: Hydractinia is easy to culture in the lab.
source: Indeed, Hydractinia is easy to culture in the lab and allows whole mount gene expression analysis, cellular analyses, transgenesis, and gene knockdown (Plickert et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hydractinia allows whole mount gene expression analysis, cellular analyses, transgenesis, and gene knockdown.
source: Indeed, Hydractinia is easy to culture in the lab and allows whole mount gene expression analysis, cellular analyses, transgenesis, and gene knockdown (Plickert et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plickert et al., 2012.

claim: Hydractinia reproduces sexually on a daily basis.
source: The animal reproduces sexually on a daily basis, but also grows clonally by elongation of gastrovascular tubes, called stolons, and asexual budding of new polyps (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the reproductive biology of the organism.

claim: Hydractinia grows clonally by elongation of gastrovascular tubes called stolons and asexual budding of new polyps.
source: The animal reproduces sexually on a daily basis, but also grows clonally by elongation of gastrovascular tubes, called stolons, and asexual budding of new polyps (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Hydractinia are small and optically translucent.
source: Finally, they are small and optically translucent, and post-metamorphic animals are sessile and can grow on microscope slides enabling in vivo imaging of cellular processes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the physical properties of the organism.

claim: Post-metamorphic Hydractinia animals are sessile and can grow on microscope slides.
source: Finally, they are small and optically translucent, and post-metamorphic animals are sessile and can grow on microscope slides enabling in vivo imaging of cellular processes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the behavior and culture properties of the organism.

claim: Hydractinia displays a remarkable regenerative ability and growth plasticity.
source: Like many cnidarians, Hydractinia displays a remarkable regenerative ability and growth plasticity, but the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying these capabilities are not well understood.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the regenerative capabilities of the organism.

claim: Stem cell migration and proliferation underlie head regeneration in Hydractinia.
source: We have studied both oral (i.e., head) and aboral (i.e., stolon) regeneration in Hydractinia and show that stem cell migration and proliferation underlie head regeneration in this animal.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stolon regeneration is achieved through a fundamentally different cellular and morphogenetic process than head regeneration.
source: Surprisingly, stolon regeneration is achieved through a fundamentally different cellular and morphogenetic process, demonstrating that a single species can apply different mechanisms to regenerate different tissues or body parts.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A single species can apply different mechanisms to regenerate different tissues or body parts.
source: Surprisingly, stolon regeneration is achieved through a fundamentally different cellular and morphogenetic process, demonstrating that a single species can apply different mechanisms to regenerate different tissues or body parts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Lesion closure by stretching out of epidermal epithelial cells occurred at both cut ends within 6 hr following decapitation in all cases.
source: Lesion closure by stretching out of epidermal epithelial cells occurred at both cut ends within 6 hr following decapitation in all cases.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments described.

claim: About 24 hr after decapitation, a dome-like tissue appeared at the oral pole.
source: About 24 hr later, a dome-like tissue appeared at the oral pole.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: A new mouth and tentacles developed 48–96 hr post decapitation in over 95% of cases.
source: This was followed by the development of a new mouth and tentacles 48–96 hr post decapitation (in over 95% of cases; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The polyps regained the ability to catch prey about two to 3 days post decapitation when a new head fully formed.
source: The polyps regained the ability to catch prey about two to 3 days post decapitation when a new head fully formed, but tentacle elongation sometimes continued for an additional few days.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Anti-acetylated tubulin antibody staining confirmed that the nervous system had completely regenerated with both neurons and nematocytes appearing normal as in control animals.
source: Anti-acetylated tubulin antibody staining confirmed that the nervous system had completely regenerated with both neurons and nematocytes (cnidarian-specific mechanosensory/effector cells) appearing normal as in control animals (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: The time course of head regeneration was variable among polyps, lasting between 1 and 4 days.
source: The time course of head regeneration (n > 300) was variable among polyps, lasting between 1 and 4 days, depending on age (young post metamorphosis animals may regenerate faster), genetic background (we use a polymorphic wild type laboratory population), and general state of health (malnourished or otherwise unhealthy animals may display delayed regeneration).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from experiments with over 300 polyps.

claim: Young post metamorphosis animals may regenerate faster.
source: The time course of head regeneration (n > 300) was variable among polyps, lasting between 1 and 4 days, depending on age (young post metamorphosis animals may regenerate faster), genetic background (we use a polymorphic wild type laboratory population), and general state of health (malnourished or otherwise unhealthy animals may display delayed regeneration).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Malnourished or otherwise unhealthy animals may display delayed regeneration.
source: The time course of head regeneration (n > 300) was variable among polyps, lasting between 1 and 4 days, depending on age (young post metamorphosis animals may regenerate faster), genetic background (we use a polymorphic wild type laboratory population), and general state of health (malnourished or otherwise unhealthy animals may display delayed regeneration).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: No indications for stolon regeneration were observed within the time course of head regeneration.
source: No indications for stolon regeneration were observed within the time course of head regeneration.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Regeneration of decapitated polyps that remained attached to their colonies was indistinguishable from isolated polyps within the natural variability.
source: Regeneration of decapitated polyps that remained attached to their colonies was indistinguishable from isolated polyps within the natural variability stated above.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Head regeneration after decapitation in the freshwater cnidarian, Hydra, can occur in the absence of cell proliferation.
source: Head regeneration after decapitation in the freshwater cnidarian, Hydra, can occur in the absence of cell proliferation (Park et al., 1970; Marcum and Campbell, 1978a, 1978b; Dübel and Schaller, 1990; Holstein et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work on Hydra.

claim: In intact Hydractinia polyps, cell proliferation was almost exclusively restricted to a band at the lower part of the polyp body column.
source: In intact Hydractinia polyps, cell proliferation was almost exclusively restricted to a band at the lower part of the polyp body column, with little or no proliferating cells outside of this band.
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation and anti-phospho-Histone 3 labeling data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A striking shift in the spatial distribution of cycling cells was evident 24–48 hpd, with cycling cells concentrated at the oral pole where the new head was about to form.
source: However, a striking shift in the spatial distribution of cycling cells was evident 24–48 hpd (hours post-decapitation). In contrast to the lower body column band-fashion distribution of cycling cells in intact polyps, the post decapitation distribution of cycling cells concentrated at the oral pole where the new head was about to form (n = 100; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 100 animals shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Intact polyps that were labeled by EdU while still connected to their stolonal network showed the same pattern of S-phase cell distribution as polyps with intact heads isolated from their colonies.
source: Intact polyps that were labeled by EdU while still connected to their stolonal network showed the same pattern of S-phase cell distribution as polyps with intact heads isolated from their colonies (n = 20; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 20 animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Head but not stolon amputation in Hydractinia is followed by the formation of a blastema with highly proliferative cells.
source: Hence, head but not stolon amputation in Hydractinia is followed by the formation of a blastema with highly proliferative cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU and pH3 labeling experiments.

claim: Epithelial cells form less than 4% of the total mitotic cell complement in both intact and regenerating animals 24 hpd.
source: We have counted mitotic cells in intact vs regenerating animals 24 hpd in three separate experiments and found that on average epithelial cells, as identified by morphology, form less than 4% of the total mitotic cell complement, whereas the vast majority of S-phase cells are i-cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from three experiments shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The vast majority of S-phase cells are i-cells.
source: We have counted mitotic cells in intact vs regenerating animals 24 hpd in three separate experiments and found that on average epithelial cells, as identified by morphology, form less than 4% of the total mitotic cell complement, whereas the vast majority of S-phase cells are i-cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from three experiments shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the relative proportion of mitotic epithelial cells in intact vs regenerating animals.
source: There was no significant difference in the relative proportion of mitotic epithelial cells in intact vs regenerating animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: I-cells form the major proliferative cellular component in Hydractinia head regeneration.
source: Hence, i-cells form the major proliferative cellular component in Hydractinia head regeneration, but the contribution of epithelial cells to this process through proliferation and/or transdifferentiation cannot be ruled out based on these data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the maceration and cell counting experiments.

claim: Absorbed doses of up to 300 Gy did not completely abolish cell proliferation in decapitated polyps.
source: We first established that absorbed doses of up to 300 Gy did not completely abolish cell proliferation in decapitated polyps (n = 30; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 30 animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 500 Gy, S-phase cells were no longer detectable.
source: At 500 Gy, S-phase cells were no longer detectable (n = 30; Figure 3—figure supplement 3) but the animals remained responsive to mechanical stimulation.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 30 animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Animals irradiated at 500 Gy remained responsive to mechanical stimulation.
source: At 500 Gy, S-phase cells were no longer detectable (n = 30; Figure 3—figure supplement 3) but the animals remained responsive to mechanical stimulation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Small numbers of apoptotic cells were found in non-irradiated animals between 6 and 24 hpd.
source: We found small numbers of apoptotic cells in non-irradiated animals between 6 and 24 hpd (n = 30).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 30 animals using TUNEL staining.

claim: Apoptotic cells play a role in the regenerative process.
source: This is consistent with previous work on other animals, where apoptotic cells were shown to play a role in the regenerative process (Hwang et al., 2004; Tseng et al., 2007; Chera et al., 2009; DuBuc et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on other animals.

claim: In irradiated animals, the distribution of apoptotic cells was similar to the distribution of proliferating i-cells in non-irradiated animals.
source: In irradiated animals, the distribution of apoptotic cells was similar to the distribution of proliferating i-cells in non-irradiated animals (n = 30; Figure 3—figure supplement 4; compare with Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 30 animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cycling i-cells are sensitive to gamma irradiation.
source: We concluded that cycling i-cells are sensitive to gamma irradiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TUNEL staining and irradiation experiments.

claim: None of the animals irradiated at 500 Gy regenerated at 48 hr following decapitation.
source: We then irradiated animals at 500 Gy followed by decapitation, and returned them to their culture tanks. None of the animals regenerated at 48 hr following this treatment (n = 30; Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 30 animals shown in Figures 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Animals irradiated at 300 Gy or lower did regenerate, but at a markedly slower pace.
source: Animals irradiated at 300 Gy or lower did regenerate, but at a markedly slower pace (n = 30; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 30 animals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No proliferative blastema developed at the oral pole of animals irradiated at 500 Gy.
source: Importantly, the lack of EdU incorporation showed that no proliferative blastema developed at the oral pole of animals irradiated at 500 Gy (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with mitomycin C had similar effects to irradiation, with animals failing to regenerate following treatment.
source: Treatment with mitomycin C, a cytostatic drug that was shown to kill i-cells in Hydractinia (Müller et al., 2004), had similar effects, with animals failing to regenerate following treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and citation to Müller et al., 2004.

claim: Cell proliferation and blastema formation are essential for Hydractinia head regeneration.
source: Therefore, cell proliferation and blastema formation are essential for Hydractinia head regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the irradiation and mitomycin C experiments.

claim: Hydractinia head regeneration is markedly different from Hydra head regeneration, which can occur through morphallaxis in the complete absence of cycling cells.
source: This is markedly different from Hydra head regeneration, which can occur through morphallaxis in the complete absence of cycling cells.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the current findings and previous work on Hydra.

claim: Piwi1, Vasa, Myc2 and Pl10 are standard stem cell markers in cnidarians and other metazoans.
source: We focused on Piwi1, Vasa, Myc2 and Pl10, all standard stem cell markers in cnidarians and other metazoans (Reddien et al., 2005; Rebscher et al., 2008; Voskoboynik et al., 2008; Alie et al., 2011; Collins et al., 2013; Juliano et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Ncol1 is an early nematocyte differentiation marker in cnidarians.
source: In addition, we studied Ncol1, an early nematocyte differentiation marker in cnidarians (David et al., 2008; Millane et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to David et al., 2008 and Millane et al., 2011.

claim: All i-cell marker genes were expressed in a band fashion at the lower part of the polyp body column, co-localizing with S-phase and mitotic cells.
source: As shown for Vasa previously (Rebscher et al., 2008), all i-cell marker genes were expressed in a band fashion at the lower part of the polyp body column, co-localizing with S-phase and mitotic cells (Figure 4A,B; compare with Figure 3A; n = 40).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 40 animals shown in Figures 4A,B and supported by citation to Rebscher et al., 2008.

claim: About 24 hpd, there was strong expression of i-cell markers and Ncol1 in the blastema.
source: Most strikingly, about 24 hpd, coinciding with the major proliferative peak in the blastema, there was strong expression of i-cell markers and Ncol1 in the blastema (n = 40; Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 40 animals shown in Figures 4C,D.

claim: The blastema that forms during head regeneration at the oral pole contains large numbers of i-cells and early nematoblasts.
source: Hence, the blastema that forms during head regeneration at the oral pole contains large numbers of i-cells and early nematoblasts in contrast to the absence of these cells in oral areas in intact animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Irradiation of animals at 500 Gy resulted in a marked reduction of i-cells and nematoblast marker expression at 24 hr post decapitation.
source: Irradiation of animals at 500 Gy resulted in a marked reduction of i-cells and nematoblast marker expression at 24 hr post decapitation (n = 10; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 10 animals shown in Figure 4E.

claim: I-cells are required for head regeneration.
source: This further shows that i-cells are sensitive to irradiation and are required for head regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the irradiation experiments.

claim: Regeneration in animals in which Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10 or Ncol1 were knocked down was compromised.
source: Regeneration in animals in which Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10 or Ncol1 were knocked down was compromised, with the frequency of regenerating RNAi animals significantly different from the control RNAi (chi-square test, p = 0.00001; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Animals treated with control (i.e., non-coding) dsRNA regenerated normally.
source: Animals treated with control (i.e., non-coding) dsRNA regenerated normally.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the control experiments.

claim: Knockdown of Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10, or Ncol1 had no visible effect on cell proliferation.
source: We found that knockdown of Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10, or Ncol1 had no visible effect on cell proliferation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: In RNAi animals the head blastema formed normally yet regeneration was significantly affected.
source: In these RNAi animals the head blastema formed normally yet regeneration was significantly affected, suggesting that these genes are required for differentiation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RNAi experiments.

claim: Piwi1, Pl10, and Vasa are required for differentiation but not for i-cell proliferation and blastema formation.
source: Hence, Piwi1, Pl10, and Vasa expression is not required for i-cell proliferation and for the formation of the head blastema.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments showing normal proliferation but impaired regeneration.

claim: Ncol1 is not expressed in cycling i-cells.
source: Ncol1, which is a nematogenesis marker, is not expressed in cycling i-cells and its downregulation is therefore not expected to affect S-phase cells.
evidence: This is based on the known function of Ncol1 as a nematogenesis marker.

claim: Knockdown of histones H2A or H4 strongly reduced EdU incorporation in regenerating animals.
source: The specificity of the RNAi treatment was further confirmed by knockdown of histones H2A or H4 which strongly reduced EdU incorporation in regenerating animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In fully grown, intact animals, i-cells are more or less restricted to the band area in the lower polyp body column, and are nearly absent from the head.
source: In fully grown, intact animals, i-cells are more or less restricted to the band area in the lower polyp body column, and are nearly absent from the head, which also does not include significant numbers of proliferating cells (n = 75/83).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 83 animals.

claim: Animals fixed 6 hpd had a strong EdU signal in the band at the lower body column and only a few EdU+ cells were scattered at more oral positions.
source: We found that animals fixed 6 hpd had a strong signal in the band at the lower body column and only a few EdU+ cells were scattered at more oral positions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by EdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Animals fixed 24 hpd had a strong EdU signal in the developed blastema.
source: However, those animals fixed 24 hpd had also a strong EdU signal in the developed blastema (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EdU pulse-chase data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EdU+ cells in the blastema must have been the very same cells that were in S-phase in the lower band 24 hr earlier and had migrated to the stump following decapitation.
source: Because no EdU could be incorporated after washing the animals, the EdU+ cells in the blastema must have been the very same cells that were in S-phase in the lower band 24 hr earlier and had migrated to the stump following decapitation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the EdU pulse-chase experiment design.

claim: S-phase cells in the band continued to proliferate even after reaching the stump and contributed new cells to the blastema through mitosis.
source: Analysis of pH3 immunoreactivity in EdU pulse chased animals revealed double positive cells in the blastema, indicating that S-phase cells in the band continued to proliferate even after reaching the stump and contributed new cells to the blastema through mitosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by double labeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP expression in transgenic polyps was consistent with the endogenous expression of Piwi1 as assessed by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry.
source: GFP expression in transgenic polyps (Figure 5C,D) was consistent with the endogenous expression of Piwi1 as assessed by in situ hybridization (Figure 4A) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figures 5C,D, 4A, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genomic integration does not occur in all cells, making the transgenic animals mosaics.
source: Because genomic integration does not occur in all cells, the animals were mosaics and not all Piwi1+ i-cells expressed GFP.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the transgenic animals.

claim: The mosaic nature of transgenic animals facilitated tracking of single cells in vivo.
source: This feature was useful because the density of GFP+ cells was not as high as would be expected in a fully transgenic animal, facilitating tracking of single cells in vivo (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is an observation about the utility of the mosaic transgenic animals shown in Figures 5C,D.

claim: Piwi1+ cells were observed migrating into the prospective head area.
source: Piwi1+ cells were observed migrating into the prospective head area (Figure 5E–G; Videos 1, 2) and no evidence for dedifferentiation was evident as all viewed recruited GFP+ cells at the blastema were migratory.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figures 5E-G and Videos 1, 2.

claim: No evidence for dedifferentiation was evident as all viewed recruited GFP+ cells at the blastema were migratory.
source: Piwi1+ cells were observed migrating into the prospective head area (Figure 5E–G; Videos 1, 2) and no evidence for dedifferentiation was evident as all viewed recruited GFP+ cells at the blastema were migratory.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the live imaging experiments shown in Figures 5E-G and Videos 1, 2.

claim: Some migrating cells underwent mitosis before reaching the blastema; they stopped migrating, completed mitosis, and the two daughter cells resumed migration.
source: Some migrating cells underwent mitosis before reaching the blastema; they stopped migrating, completed mitosis, and the two daughter cells resumed migration (Figure 5G; Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from live imaging shown in Figure 5G and Video 2.

claim: The primary cellular source for establishing the head blastema and head regeneration is migration of i-cells from the band in the polyp lower body column to the prospective head area.
source: Based on these experiments and the EdU pulse-chasing, we conclude that the primary cellular source for establishing the head blastema and, subsequently, head regeneration is migration of i-cells from the band in the polyp lower body column to the prospective head area.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU pulse-chase and live imaging experiments.

claim: A possible contribution of existing epithelial cells to the regeneration process through mitosis and/or transdifferentiation cannot be ruled out.
source: A possible contribution of existing epithelial cells to the regeneration process through mitosis and/or transdifferentiation (body column epithelial cells to tentacle epithelial cells) cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging limitations of the current data.

claim: Hydractinia polyps are not able to regenerate stolons directly from their aboral ends.
source: Hydractinia polyps are not able to regenerate stolons directly from their aboral ends (Müller et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller et al., 1986.

claim: Polyps, or even fragments of them, can transform into stolons.
source: Polyps, or even fragments of them, can, instead, transform into stolons but this phenomenon is not well understood (Putnam Hazen, 1902; Müller et al., 1986; Lange and Müller, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Putnam Hazen, 1902; Müller et al., 1986; Lange and Müller, 1991.

claim: Isolated polyps healed the cut surface within hours.
source: Isolated polyps healed the cut surface within hours (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The polyps appeared normal for days and sometimes weeks, responded to mechanical stimuli by contraction, and were able to catch, kill, and ingest brine shrimp nauplii.
source: The polyps appeared normal for days and sometimes weeks, responded to mechanical stimuli by contraction, and were able to catch, kill, and ingest brine shrimp nauplii, resembling a solitary Hydra polyp.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: No blastema developed at the aboral pole after stolon removal.
source: No blastema developed at the aboral pole after stolon removal, and the general distribution of EdU+ cells was largely similar to polyps that were labeled on their colony. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over the next weeks, the polyps started resorbing their tentacles and thereby lost the ability to feed.
source: Over the next weeks, however, the polyps started resorbing their tentacles and thereby lost the ability to feed (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The entire head structure disappeared and each polyp's cylindrical body column started to elongate, thereby decreasing its diameter.
source: Next, the entire head structure disappeared and each polyp's cylindrical body column started to elongate, thereby decreasing its diameter (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: New branches appeared at irregular intervals and some developed into polyps with fully functional heads and tentacles, thereby regaining the ability to feed.
source: New branches appeared at irregular intervals and some developed into polyps with fully functional heads and tentacles, thereby regaining the ability to feed (n = 200; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from 200 polyps shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Chitin secretion (which is stolon specific in Hydractinia) commenced.
source: Chitin secretion (which is stolon specific in Hydractinia) (Lange and Müller, 1991) commenced (Figure 6C) and eventually, sexual polyps developed and produced fertile gametes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6C and supported by citation to Lange and Müller, 1991.

claim: Sexual polyps developed and produced fertile gametes.
source: Chitin secretion (which is stolon specific in Hydractinia) (Lange and Müller, 1991) commenced (Figure 6C) and eventually, sexual polyps developed and produced fertile gametes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The polyp body column had transformed into stolons rather than regenerated new stolons from the aboral stump.
source: Based on chitin secretion and ability to generate polyps, it appeared that the polyp body column had transformed into stolons rather than regenerated new stolons from the aboral stump.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of chitin secretion and polyp budding.

claim: Wnt3 is an established oral marker in Hydractinia.
source: Wnt3 is an established oral marker in Hydractinia (Plickert et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2007; Duffy et al., 2010), but is also expressed weakly in the i-cell band of polyps (Plickert et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Plickert et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2007; Duffy et al., 2010.

claim: Wnt3 is also expressed weakly in the i-cell band of polyps.
source: Wnt3 is an established oral marker in Hydractinia (Plickert et al., 2006; Müller et al., 2007; Duffy et al., 2010), but is also expressed weakly in the i-cell band of polyps (Plickert et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plickert et al., 2006.

claim: Polyp heads that were losing their tentacles had also lost Wnt3 expression.
source: We found that polyp heads that were losing their tentacles had also lost Wnt3 expression (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Wnt3 mRNA reappeared in the oral tip of new polyps budding from the newly transformed tissue.
source: By contrast, Wnt3 mRNA reappeared in the oral tip of new polyps budding from this newly transformed tissue (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Loss of oral Wnt3 expression preceded, or accompanied, the loss of head characteristics such as tentacles and mouth.
source: Hence, loss of oral Wnt3 expression preceded, or accompanied, the loss of head characteristics such as tentacles and mouth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Wnt3 expression analysis during polyp to stolon transformation.

claim: In normal, non-regenerating polyps, i-cells were largely restricted to the band area at the polyp lower body column.
source: In normal, non-regenerating polyps, i-cells were largely restricted to the band area at the polyp lower body column (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In stolons, i-cells were equally distributed in the epidermal interstices along the stolon flanks.
source: In stolons, by contrast, i-cells were equally distributed in the epidermal interstices along the stolon flanks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isolated polyps that lost head structures showed a stolon-like expression pattern of Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10, Myc2 and Ncol1.
source: Indeed, in situ hybridization of Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10, Myc2 and Ncol1 on isolated polyps that lost head structures showed a stolon-like expression pattern of these genes (Figure 6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hydractinia aboral regeneration proceeds through three stages: First, loss of anterior-posterior polarity; second, full transformation of the polyp into a stolon; third, budding new polyps and regaining oral-aboral polarity.
source: To summarize this point, Hydractinia aboral regeneration is not direct and proceeds through three stages: First, loss of anterior-posterior polarity; second, full transformation of the polyp into a stolon; third, budding new polyps and regaining oral-aboral polarity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the observations of polyp to stolon transformation.

claim: Hydractinia polyps can regenerate a head through i-cell migration and blastema formation, but they cannot directly regenerate stolons; they can transform into stolonal tissue instead.
source: Hence, Hydractinia polyps can regenerate a head through i-cell migration and blastema formation, but they cannot directly regenerate stolons; they can transform into stolonal tissue instead.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the main findings of the study.

claim: Decapitation was followed by rapid wound healing that primarily involved stretching of epithelial cells without the requirement for cell proliferation.
source: Decapitation was followed by rapid wound healing that primarily involved stretching of epithelial cells without the requirement for cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Not all i-cells migrate to the stump, consistent with migratory vs non-migratory i-cell sub-populations.
source: Of note, our data show that not all i-cells migrate to the stump, consistent with migratory vs non-migratory i-cell sub-populations.
evidence: This is an observation from the migration experiments.

claim: New head structures developed within 2–3 days, after which most i-cells disappeared from the head area and resumed their normal position in the band.
source: New head structures developed within 2–3 days, after which most i-cells disappeared from the head area and resumed their normal position in the band.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: The role of Piwi1, Vasa and Pl10 might be related to the ability of i-cells to differentiate rather than to keeping them undifferentiated.
source: Hence, the role of these genes might be related to the ability of i-cells to differentiate rather than to keeping them undifferentiated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments showing normal proliferation but impaired regeneration.

claim: Similar results were obtained with Smedwi2 (a Piwi homologue) knockdown in planarians.
source: Similar results were obtained with Smedwi2 (a Piwi homologue) knockdown in planarians (Reddien et al., 2005), but knocking out a different stem cell gene, Sox2, in axolotl inhibits proliferation of neural progenitors (Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reddien et al., 2005 and Fei et al., 2014.

claim: Knocking out Sox2 in axolotl inhibits proliferation of neural progenitors.
source: Similar results were obtained with Smedwi2 (a Piwi homologue) knockdown in planarians (Reddien et al., 2005), but knocking out a different stem cell gene, Sox2, in axolotl inhibits proliferation of neural progenitors (Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fei et al., 2014.

claim: A common view in the literature has been that cnidarians can regenerate through morphallaxis, that is, without contribution from cell proliferation.
source: A common view in the literature has been that cnidarians can regenerate through morphallaxis, that is, without contribution from cell proliferation (Park et al., 1970; Marcum and Campbell, 1978a, 1978b; Holstein et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: More recent studies conducted on Hydra and on the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis have shown that cell proliferation accompanies the regeneration of cnidarian heads under normal circumstances.
source: More recent studies conducted on Hydra and on the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, however, have shown that cell proliferation accompanies the regeneration of cnidarian heads under normal circumstances (Govindasamy et al., 2014), but the necessity of proliferation was only demonstrated in Nematostella decapitation and Hydra bisection (Miljkovic-Licina et al., 2007; Chera et al., 2009; Passamaneck and Martindale, 2012; DuBuc et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work on Hydra and Nematostella.

claim: The necessity of proliferation was only demonstrated in Nematostella decapitation and Hydra bisection.
source: More recent studies conducted on Hydra and on the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, however, have shown that cell proliferation accompanies the regeneration of cnidarian heads under normal circumstances (Govindasamy et al., 2014), but the necessity of proliferation was only demonstrated in Nematostella decapitation and Hydra bisection (Miljkovic-Licina et al., 2007; Chera et al., 2009; Passamaneck and Martindale, 2012; DuBuc et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miljkovic-Licina et al., 2007; Chera et al., 2009; Passamaneck and Martindale, 2012; DuBuc et al., 2014.

claim: The results support the new emerging view on head regeneration in the Cnidaria.
source: Our results support the new emerging view on head regeneration in the Cnidaria and are consistent with Passamaneck and Martindale's hypothesis (Passamaneck and Martindale, 2012) that Hydra's ability to regenerate a head in the absence of cell proliferation is evolutionarily derived within this phylum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings in the context of recent literature.

claim: Hydra's ability to regenerate a head in the absence of cell proliferation is evolutionarily derived within the Cnidaria phylum.
source: Our results support the new emerging view on head regeneration in the Cnidaria and are consistent with Passamaneck and Martindale's hypothesis (Passamaneck and Martindale, 2012) that Hydra's ability to regenerate a head in the absence of cell proliferation is evolutionarily derived within this phylum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Passamaneck and Martindale, 2012 and the current findings.

claim: Blastema formation is an evolutionarily primitive hallmark of distal regeneration in animals.
source: This scenario suggests that blastema formation is an evolutionarily primitive hallmark of distal regeneration in animals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the current findings and comparative analysis.

claim: Downregulation of Wnt3 or Tcf in decapitated polyps induces phenotypes reminiscent of polyp to stolon transformation.
source: In a previous study, it has been shown that Wnt signaling promotes oral structures in Hydractinia, but represses stolons (Duffy et al., 2010). Downregulation of Wnt3 or Tcf in decapitated polyps induces phenotypes reminiscent of polyp to stolon transformation in the present study, but requires shorter time to develop (Duffy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2010.

claim: Wnt signaling promotes oral structures in Hydractinia, but represses stolons.
source: In a previous study, it has been shown that Wnt signaling promotes oral structures in Hydractinia, but represses stolons (Duffy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2010.

claim: Wnt3 expression and oral-aboral polarity are lost spontaneously in isolated polyps.
source: We show that in the absence of experimental manipulation, Wnt3 expression and oral-aboral polarity are lost spontaneously in isolated polyps, enabling the transformation of the polyp into stolonal tissue that can bud new polyps.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Wnt3 not only maintains oral- but also polyp- identity, and stolons develop by default in its absence.
source: Possibly, Wnt3 not only maintains oral- but also polyp- identity, and stolons develop by default in its absence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observations of Wnt3 expression and polyp to stolon transformation.

claim: The mechanisms governing animal regeneration can be not only species-specific, but also tissue-specific within a single species.
source: In conclusion, our results, and results published over the past few years by others (Chera et al., 2009; Kragl et al., 2009; DuBuc et al., 2014; Sandoval-Guzman et al., 2014), show that the mechanisms governing animal regeneration can be not only species-specific, but also tissue-specific within a single species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and cited work.

claim: Some regeneration mechanisms, like blastema formation, are conserved in animals.
source: Some regeneration mechanisms, like blastema formation, are conserved in animals, and their modulation over evolutionary times may have affected the regenerative ability of different species.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparative analysis of regeneration mechanisms.

claim: Modulation of conserved regeneration mechanisms over evolutionary times may have affected the regenerative ability of different species.
source: Some regeneration mechanisms, like blastema formation, are conserved in animals, and their modulation over evolutionary times may have affected the regenerative ability of different species.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: The sessile nature of adult Hydractinia facilitates long-term studies at single cell resolution.
source: An exciting development in the study of regeneration is provided by the ability to track individual, transgenic cells in vivo using Hydractinia as an animal model. In vivo cell migration assays have been performed in Hydra (Khalturin et al., 2007), but the sessile nature of adult Hydractinia facilitates long-term studies at single cell resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of Hydractinia as a model system, supported by citation to Khalturin et al., 2007.

claim: In vivo cell migration assays have been performed in Hydra.
source: In vivo cell migration assays have been performed in Hydra (Khalturin et al., 2007), but the sessile nature of adult Hydractinia facilitates long-term studies at single cell resolution.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Khalturin et al., 2007.

claim: Hydrozoan stem cells are called interstitial cells, or i-cells for short.
source: Hydrozoan stem cells are called interstitial cells, or i-cells for short.
evidence: This is a definition of terminology.

claim: In Hydractinia, i-cells reside in interstitial spaces between epithelial cells (mostly epidermal).
source: In Hydractinia, i-cells reside in interstitial spaces between epithelial cells (mostly epidermal), and at a population level are thought to be pluripotent life long, giving rise to all somatic lineages as well as germ cells (Müller et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller et al., 2004.

claim: At a population level, i-cells are thought to be pluripotent life long, giving rise to all somatic lineages as well as germ cells.
source: In Hydractinia, i-cells reside in interstitial spaces between epithelial cells (mostly epidermal), and at a population level are thought to be pluripotent life long, giving rise to all somatic lineages as well as germ cells (Müller et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller et al., 2004.

claim: In Hydra, i-cells do not contribute to the two self-renewing epithelial lineages.
source: This is very different from Hydra where i-cells do not contribute to the two self-renewing epithelial lineages (Bode, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bode, 1996.

claim: Hydractinia polyps possess tissue pluripotency.
source: The newly transformed stolons budded new polyps and became fully functional, sexually mature colonies. These data, therefore, show that Hydractinia polyps possess tissue pluripotency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that transformed stolons can bud new polyps and form functional colonies.

claim: Cnidarians have relatively few cell types including epidermal and gastrodermal myoepithelial cells, several types of neurons, stinging cells (nematocytes), gland cells, and stem cells.
source: Cnidarians have relatively few cell types including epidermal and gastrodermal myoepithelial cells, several types of neurons, stinging cells (nematocytes), gland cells, and stem cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement about cnidarian cell types shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mitomycin C is a cytostatic drug that was shown to kill i-cells in Hydractinia.
source: Treatment with mitomycin C, a cytostatic drug that was shown to kill i-cells in Hydractinia (Müller et al., 2004), had similar effects, with animals failing to regenerate following treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller et al., 2004.

claim: Colonies of H. echinata were cultured in artificial seawater at 18°C under 14/10 light/dark regime.
source: Colonies of H. echinata were cultured in artificial seawater at 18°C under 14/10 light/dark regime.
evidence: This is a description of the culture conditions used in the study.

claim: Colonies were fed brine shrimp nauplii four times a week and ground fish once a week.
source: They were fed brine shrimp nauplii four times a week and ground fish once a week.
evidence: This is a description of the feeding protocol used in the study.

claim: Gamma-irradiation was carried out using a 137Cs source at a dose-rate of 12 Gy/min.
source: Gamma-irradiation was carried out using a 137Cs source at a dose-rate of 12 Gy/min.
evidence: This is a description of the irradiation method used in the study.

claim: In situ hybridization was performed at 55°C.
source: In situ hybridization was performed at 55°C.
evidence: This is a description of the in situ hybridization protocol used in the study.

claim: RNAi was performed with polyps incubated in seawater containing 30–50 ng/μl double stranded RNA.
source: Briefly, polyps were removed from their colony and were then decapitated. Following decapitation the cylindrical body columns were incubated in seawater containing 30–50 ng/μl double stranded RNA (dsRNA) corresponding to 200 bp coding sequence of Piwi1, Vasa, Pl10 and Ncol1.
evidence: This is a description of the RNAi protocol used in the study.

claim: qPCR analysis of Piwi1 RNAi treated regenerating animals revealed a significant reduction in Piwi1 mRNA levels comparing to control RNAi.
source: qPCR analysis of Piwi1 RNAi treated regenerating animals revealed a significant reduction in Piwi1 mRNA levels comparing to control RNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: One-cell stage embryos were microinjected with 200 pl volume of the plasmid at a concentration of 4–5 μg/μl.
source: One-cell stage embryos were microinjected with 200 pl volume of the plasmid at a concentration of 4–5 μg/μl as previously described (Künzel et al., 2010; Millane et al., 2011; Duffy, 2012; Kanska and Frank, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the microinjection protocol used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: Genomic integration and stable GFP expression occurs in Hydractinia within 24 hr.
source: Genomic integration and stable GFP expression occurs in Hydractinia within 24 hr (Künzel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Künzel et al., 2010.

claim: For time-lapse videos, images or stacks were taken every 5 min.
source: For time-lapse videos, images or stacks were taken every 5 min.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging protocol used in the study.

claim: EdU incorporation was performed for 20–60 min at a concentration of 150 μM.
source: EdU incorporation was performed for 20–60 min at a concentration of 150 μM.
evidence: This is a description of the EdU labeling protocol used in the study.
